1:
Clarke sets out the chapter in six parts: the uncleanness of men, the mode of their cleansing, uncleanness accidental and casual, the uncleanness of women, the mode of their cleansing, and a recapitulation. Ellicott counts the matter more exactly, as two diseased and three natural secretions. Gill notes that Aaron is addressed along with Moses, since some of these purifications depended on the priest. He adds, from the same authority, that the laws bound the children of Israel only and not the Gentiles. Henry describes the disease with disgust rather than diagnosis. It was usually the effect of wantonness and a dissolute course of life, filling a man's bones with the sins of his youth and leaving him to mourn at the last, when the pleasures of his wickedness have vanished and nothing remains but a rotten carcase and a wounded conscience. Wesley says the same in a line, calling it the running of the reins and generally the consequence of sin. Calvin ranges wider, treating the whole chapter as a supplement that might be appended to the seventh commandment.

What the word flesh means here divides two of them squarely. Ellicott takes it as a euphemism for the private parts, as frequently elsewhere, and would render the clause his issue is unclean rather than because of his issue he is unclean. Keil and Delitzsch deny the euphemism. Their argument is a cross-reference: the later verse orders the man to bathe his flesh in water, which cannot mean one organ only. They add that the issue is not described clearly enough for anyone to determine with certainty what disease is meant. Clarke will not guess either, though he reports that some take it for the consequence of a very bad infection or of criminal indulgence, since it could be communicated in so many ways.

How far the defilement travelled is where the rabbinic detail gathers. Gill reports from the Mishnah that such a man defiles a bed five ways — standing, sitting, lying, hanging and leaning — and that a bed so defiled infects a man in seven, adding touching and bearing. Ellicott gives the same five and then presses them to their limit. The patient's polluting power was held so great that he defiled a bed through a stone laid over it, and if he set one foot on each of two beds he defiled both. The loathing shows elsewhere too. Even the physician who had to examine him professionally was defiled for the rest of the day, and had to wash his clothes and immerse his whole body before returning to his own sacred privileges.

The remaining clauses are read as extensions of the same principle. Ellicott explains the spitting from custom: to spit in the face was, and is, a common Oriental expression of contempt, and a man in this condition would be the more irritable and the readier to use it. Gill takes the case as accidental rather than deliberate, and hears in it a figure of all corrupt communication out of the mouth of evil men, which defiles the speaker and his company alike. On the saddle Ellicott prefers any carriage, noting that the masculine form occurs only three times while the feminine occurs forty-four and is always rendered chariot; he understands the seat within a palanquin, so that the bearers who carry it are defiled as well. He observes that the rinsing of hands here is the only place in the law where washing the hands alone is prescribed to stop pollution spreading, and Wesley adds that this shorter course served only if it was done speedily. On the vessels the reasoning turns practical. Earthenware was broken and wood only rinsed, and Ellicott notes that the law, which so often considers what people can afford, mercifully spares the more costly utensils.
13:
Cleansed here means healed, not yet purified. Gill and Wesley both gloss it as the ceasing of the issue, and Ellicott is explicit that the real purification waited on the ritual of these three verses. The seven days he explains as a trial period, allowing time to be sure the infirmity had actually gone. If any vestige appeared within them, or even at the end of the seventh day after the man had bathed, he had to begin and count seven more. Keil and Delitzsch give the same sequence more briefly. Ellicott adds a note on the water, which is literally living water — that is, running water rather than standing.

The offering is where Ellicott finds the chapter's severity plainest. Elsewhere two turtledoves or two young pigeons were the concession allowed to the poor, who could not afford better. Here that meanest offering is prescribed for everyone alike, with no option of bringing a costlier sacrifice. He gathers the rest of the severity from outside the chapter. Such men were put outside the camp, and under the second Temple were barred from the Passover meal and banished from the holy city. When David wished the worst on his adversaries he prayed that the house of Joab might never lack one that had an issue. On the atonement Ellicott and Wesley differ in emphasis. Ellicott makes it atonement for the sinful act that brought the infirmity on; Wesley denies the condition was itself a sin, calling it rather the punishment of sin, though often sinful enough as the fruit of intemperance.

The second case is involuntary and much lighter. Gill distinguishes it carefully: not lawful cohabitation, and not any criminal act, but what comes through a dream or a lustful imagination. Ellicott notes that the man had only to immerse himself the next morning and remain unclean till sundown. He observes that the ancients did much the same, the Egyptian priests bathing when defiled by a dream, and the Koran forbidding a Mahommedan his prayers until he has performed the prescribed washing. Garments and skins that were touched had to be washed, skin meaning here what a man wears or lies upon as distinct from cloth; and Ellicott hears the apostle borrowing from this very clause when he speaks of hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.

The last verse of the group is disputed, and the dispute is not small. Keil and Delitzsch are careful about what is being called unclean: it was not the act as such, as many erroneously suppose, but the emission of seed in it. Ellicott takes the plain sense and does not soften it, that even between a man and his lawful wife the act pollutes both, so that both must bathe and remain unclean till sundown and be barred from the sanctuary that day. From this, he says, came the rule that abstinence was a necessary preparation for sacred duties, since he who had approached his wife could not draw near to God. Clarke sees a purpose in the inconvenience, since the pains, separations and privations involved would keep men from making an unlawful use of lawful things. Wesley refuses the whole reading. He would understand the verse of the man with the issue only, and argues that to make ordinary marriage defiling is contrary to the whole current of scripture, which calls the marriage bed undefiled, contrary to the practice of the Jews, and contrary to the light of nature and reason.
19:
Having finished what was to be said of the male, Gill notes with Aben Ezra, the Scripture now begins with the female. Calvin distinguishes two kinds of issue. With almost all women it occurs every month; some labour under a constant hemorrhage. Both are declared unclean, and the separation runs longer if the blood flows beyond the usual time. Wesley reads "in her flesh" as in her secret parts, taking flesh as it was taken at the head of the chapter, so that the verse notes her monthly disease. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the discharge does not as a rule last more than four or five days. The seven days were therefore fixed on account of the significance of the number seven. Ellicott likewise makes the seven days cover exceptional cases, as in the first stage after childbirth. Wesley marks the limit of the putting apart. She was not sent out of the camp. She was separated from converse with her husband and others, and from access to the house of God.

Ellicott will not have the law read without its background. To appreciate its mercy one must remember the gross superstitions of the ancients about women in this condition. It was believed that if such a woman sat under a tree all its fruit fell off. At her approach the edge of a tool was blunted. Copper vessels contracted a fetid smell and meat turned sour. The Parsees forbade her to speak to anyone, and those who brought her food set it down at a distance. The Zabii purified with fire every place she had trodden. Even the wind blowing from her quarter was held to pollute. At the River La Plata they are sewn into hammocks with only a small aperture for the mouth. It was to restrain the Jews from these superstitions and these inhuman acts that the Lawgiver ordained rules so benign.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the degrees of the defilement. She made unclean everyone who touched her, everything she lay or sat upon, everyone who touched her bed or her seat, and anyone who touched the blood upon them. All these were unclean until evening, and had to wash their clothes and bathe. Ellicott grades the contact further at verse twenty-three. Touching the bed or seat itself required washing of clothes, bathing, and pollution till sundown. Touching a vessel merely lying upon that bed required only uncleanness till sundown, with no washing at all. The defilement in that case is not primary but secondary. Gill limits the separation to the bed: she might still be with her husband and do all offices for him. Wesley limits the touching to grown persons. The infant she might suckle was exempted by the greater law of necessity, and by that earlier law which required women to give suck to their own children.

The last case is a man who lies with her. Gill takes it with Aben Ezra of one who did so ignorantly, since he who lay with her wilfully was guilty of cutting off. Clarke and Wesley reconcile the seven days here with the death sentence of the twentieth chapter the same way. There both parties knew the situation; here the circumstance was not known till afterwards. Clarke adds the general opinion that offspring so obtained is infected with diseases from which their posterity is scarcely ever freed. Wesley presses the public injury too, to the commonwealth and to the honour of true religion. Keil and Delitzsch will not soften the verse into sharing a bed; the parallels require conjugal intercourse. Henry recalls the woman who had spent her estate on physicians for twelve years and was cured by touching the hem of Christ's garment. He notes too that idolatry is compared to the uncleanness of a removed woman, and that Jerusalem, her filthiness in her skirts, was shunned as one.
25:
The last case is the chronic one. Ellicott calls it an issue arising from a derangement of the constitution, and identifies it with the complaint of the woman who came to Christ. Gill says the same, and marks what makes it extraordinary: it falls outside the time of her separation, and by the Targum of Jonathan it must continue three days at least. Sometimes it ran for years, as with the woman whom Christ cured after twelve. Keil and Delitzsch read the two clauses as two cases. The blood may flow many days away from the time of her monthly uncleanness, or it may flow on beyond that time. Either way she was unclean as long as it lasted, exactly as in the days of her separation.

Nothing in the earlier rules is relaxed for the longer trouble. Gill says her bed is as defiled and as defiling as the bed of her separation. Keil and Delitzsch extend it to her seat and to everyone who touched her or these things. Gill notes that where the Hebrew has whoever touches those things, the Septuagint reads whoever touches her. Ellicott then turns to the cure, and takes cleansed here in the sense it bore of the man: not purified, but healed, the disappearance of the complaint. From its cessation she counts seven days in which no trace may be observed, as in the case of the less innocent disorder. Wesley gives the reason for the interval plainly. It was for trial, whether this was only a temporary obstruction or a real cessation. Gill dates the eighth day from the healing, or at least from the day she began to number.

Her offering is the man's. Ellicott sets the two side by side and finds one difference only: the man had also to bathe in living water, because he had brought his illness upon himself. Clarke will not let the sacrifices pass as mere ritual. In all these cases moral pollution was considered more or less present, since even such infirmities sprang from the original defection of man. That is why one bird was offered for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. Gill reads the atonement as typical, pointing to Christ, who by himself purged our sins, and takes the design of the whole set of laws to be the exposure of the filthiness of sin. That filthiness rises from the corruption of human nature, and the pollution of fleshly lusts in particular. What is required is purification by the grace of God and the blood of Christ, and holiness of heart and life, before a man may draw near to God in public worship. Keil and Delitzsch find the same demand in the verb of the charge that follows, which means to make a person keep aloof from a thing, and so here deliverance from the state of uncleanness.
31:
The chapter ends with its own reason. Ellicott points out who is charged with it: the ye of the verse is Moses and Aaron, to whom these laws were addressed together at the outset. They are to restrain Israel, lest the people be punished with death for approaching the Lord in a defiled state. He would render the last word dwelling place rather than tabernacle. Gill offers two senses of the separating. It may mean setting them apart because of their uncleanness and while they remain in it, from other persons, even their nearest relations, and from the house of God. Or it may mean teaching them by these rules to separate themselves, and to be careful to keep apart while the impurity lasts. He notes that only the children of Israel are named, since the laws bound them with their proselytes and servants, and not the Gentiles.

Clarke reads the charge on two levels at once. The separation made the trouble less frequent and kept any contagion from spreading, as pest-houses and fever-wards keep the infected from the sound. So life was prolonged by these prudential cares. But the unclean man was also kept from presuming to enter the tabernacle before he was purified, lest he provoke divine justice to consume him while worshipping with a polluted mind and impure hands. Wesley takes the defiling the same double way. It was ceremonial, by coming into the sanctuary unclean, and moral, by contempt of God's express command to cleanse themselves. He then states the grand reason of all these laws. Israel was taught its privilege, that they were purified unto God as a peculiar people, so that what defiled them defiled no one else. They were taught their duty at the same time, to keep themselves clean from all pollutions.

Gill takes the last two verses for a recapitulation of the whole chapter. He lingers on the phrase for the woman's courses, which the text calls a sickness. The word is elsewhere rendered languid and faint, and some would render it here in pain; and pains are reckoned among the signs of the condition by the Mishnic doctors. He adds that the man who lies with her that is unclean means her own husband. Clarke closes with the chapter itself. How unpromising and forbidding it looks at first view, and how full it proves of wise, humane and moral regulations. God has purity of heart continually in view: to keep the soul holy he cuts off the occasions of sin, hedging up the way with briars and thorns until transgression is painful, shameful and expensive. Preventing grace, Clarke concludes, is not less necessary than the grace that saves and preserves.
